extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of Montaigne / literary readers
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading of Montaigne's Essays (English translation) covering moral/philosophical judgments about suicide, courage, conscience, prudence, and related human behaviours. The text presents principles illustrated by classical and historical examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bravery vs fear of future ills
rubrics_metrics.description: True bravery is to 'boldly dare withstand the mischiefs he apprehends, when they confront him and can be deferred.' Fear of future ills often makes men run into extreme danger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne cites Lucan: the wise response to feared harms is to face them when they arrive rather than be driven by anticipatory fear into rash acts. Example/contrast: those who, through fear of the future, make themselves run into extreme danger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-contempt is unnatural and vain
rubrics_metrics.description: It is against nature for a man to contemn and make little account of himself; desiring to be something other than what one is is a vanity that effects nothing for the desirer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues that being alive is all we have and that wishing to be an angel, for instance, does nothing for the living person; thus self-hatred or contempt is a human disease not found in other creatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid suicide to secure an unrealized 'peace'
rubrics_metrics.description: Security, indolence, and avoidance of life's evils purchased by dying give no advantage if the person will not enjoy peace (i.e., if death removes capacity to enjoy the supposed benefit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: 'that man evades war to very little purpose who can have no fruition of peace.' Suicide to avoid trouble is pointless if one cannot enjoy the repose allegedly gained by death.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on 'reasonable exit' (justifications for self-murder)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although some schools call suicide 'A reasonable exit' under certain circumstances, there must be limits; not every discomfort or trivial cause justifies killing oneself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne records debates among ancient authorities (e.g., Diogenes Laertius on Zeno). He condemns mass or fantastical suicides (Milesian virgins) and implies that community persuasion can produce terrible excesses; therefore any allowance for self-murder must be narrowly and carefully defined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve life while there remains hope
rubrics_metrics.description: One should not throw away life while there is an 'inch of hope' remaining, because fortune often turns unexpectedly and brings relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Cleomenes rejects counsel to die while hope remains; Josephus is saved after maintaining hope amid apparent doom; Brutus and Cassius are reproached for premature suicide. Montaigne uses gladiator and Virgil quotes to illustrate the reversibility of fortune.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suicide can be honorable to avoid dishonor or serve country
rubrics_metrics.description: In some cases suicide may be an act of honour or virtue (e.g., to avoid an ignominious life, to preserve dignity, or to serve one's country).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: Cleomenes choosing a death 'of use to his country', Ninachetuen's ritual self-immolation to preserve honour, Vibius Virrius and the senators' collective suicide to avoid surrender. Montaigne treats these as complex, sometimes laudable acts tied to cultural notions of honour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severe, prolonged physical pain as most excusable motive
rubrics_metrics.description: Pain and fear of a worse death are the most excusable incitements to suicide; classical authorities (e.g., Pliny, Seneca) limit justifiable suicide to grave bodily maladies or long discomposing conditions of the soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pliny's (reported) list of diseases for which men historically killed themselves (stone in the bladder, severe stomach pain, headache) and Seneca's note about long-term disorders. Montaigne signals that extreme, chronic suffering is a different moral case than many other motives for self-killing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary death from the desire for a greater good (religious hope) is not necessarily despair
rubrics_metrics.description: A voluntary dissolution may arise from eager hope (e.g., the desire to be with Christ) rather than from despair; such death can proceed from calm and deliberate judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: St. Paul's wish 'to be with Christ' and Cleombrotus of Ambracia who, after reading Plato's Phaedo, drowned himself out of desire for the afterlife. Montaigne cautions against bluntly labelling all self-killing as 'despair.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Societal/legal regulation of voluntary death
rubrics_metrics.description: Some governments regulate and control the justice and opportunity of voluntary death—permitting it only with magistrate oversight or public justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: Marseilles kept public hemlock for those who petitioned the senate and obtained leave; other places had similar laws. Montaigne notes such communal/legal practices as limiting suicides and imposing procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudence in delaying reception of information ('Business to-morrow')
rubrics_metrics.description: It can be prudent to defer reading or reacting to new information out of respect for others or to avoid interrupting present affairs, but deferring important information for personal convenience (negligence) is culpable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdotes: Plutarch's Rusticus defers opening a packet until a declamation ends (commended for gravity/civility but possibly imprudent if the letter contained urgent matters); Caesar nearly lost chance to save himself by deferring a warning. Montaigne contrasts respectful deferment with negligent delay that can harm one's interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for privacy of letters / avoid prying
rubrics_metrics.description: One should not open letters directed to another, even if fortune guides them into one's hand; to do so is an intrusion Montaigne avoids and condemns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne states he never opens letters not addressed to him and is angry with himself if he unintentionally reads someone else's letter. He presents this as a moral practice of respect and restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscience as internal judge and tormentor
rubrics_metrics.description: Conscience reveals and punishes the guilty by creating inner torment, accusations, and imaginations that betray secrets and make one suffer as if punished already.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: a guilty conscience makes one imagine exposure (Bessus and the sparrows), sleep-talking or delirium exposing crimes, Apollodorus's dream; citations from Juvenal, Lucretius, and Epicurus. Montaigne argues conscience is a primary punishment and can force self-accusation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good conscience produces confidence and steadiness
rubrics_metrics.description: A good conscience grants assurance and courage, allowing a person to face hazards with steadiness because of knowledge of one's own innocence and intentions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Scipio's composed responses to accusations (refusing to abase himself, tearing up his account-book rather than grovel), which Montaigne attributes to the confidence of a clear conscience. He uses classical citations to support the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Torture/rack as an unreliable test of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The rack is a dangerous, uncertain invention because pain can make both guilty and innocent confess or lie; it tests endurance rather than truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues that pain will make even the innocent lie ('Etiam innocentes cogit mentiri dolor') and cites many false confessions (e.g., Philotas) to show that torture produces unreliable results and often kills while failing to find truth.
